explain.say: Here is a strange fact: you are surrounded by nitrogen, 78% of the air, and your body needs it to build proteins. Yet neither you nor plants can use it straight from the air! Tiny bacteria solve this. Let's go round the cycle.

explain.say: Look at the top: nitrogen gas in the air. Now the next stage. Special bacteria live in little lumps on the roots of peas, beans and lentils, called root nodules. They fix nitrogen, which means turning the gas into a form plants can use. Isn't that clever?

faq.q: Why can't plants use nitrogen from the air?
faq.a: Nitrogen gas is made of two atoms held by a very strong triple bond, so it hardly reacts. Plants can only take in nitrogen as nitrates or ammonium from the soil.
asks: Tell me about nitrogen in the air

faq.a: They turn nitrogen gas into ammonia, which plants can use. Some live free in soil; others, like Rhizobium, live in root nodules of legumes such as peas, beans, lentils and clover. Lightning also fixes a little nitrogen.
Nitrifying bacteria in the soil turn ammonia, from decay and waste, first into nitrites and then into nitrates, which plant roots absorb.
In waterlogged soil with little oxygen, denitrifying bacteria turn nitrates back into nitrogen gas, which returns to the air. This makes soil less fertile.

faq.q: Why do farmers grow beans to improve soil?
faq.a: Beans and other legumes have nitrogen-fixing bacteria in their roots. When the plants are ploughed back in, they add nitrogen to the soil, so the next crop needs less fertiliser. This is part of crop rotation.

facts: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the air.
Rhizobium bacteria in the root nodules of legumes fix nitrogen gas into ammonia.
